questions.question: Explain how soils contribute to the global carbon cycle. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how soils contribute to the global carbon cycle. [U]/ [CO3]

  • top 30 cm than the atmosphere and vegetation combined. Carbon is
  • transferred to the soil via roots, leaves, and other debris. Soil organic matter
  • (SOM) is the main component.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the feeding strategies of macrofauna detritivores (earthworms, millipedes) versus mesofauna detritivores (springtails, mites). / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare and contrast the feeding strategies of macrofauna detritivores [U]/ [CO2]
  • (earthworms, millipedes) versus mesofauna detritivores (springtails, mites).
  • Earthworm and millipedes are both crucial detrit tivores and are essential
  • members of the detritus food web. Millipedes primarily act as “shredders”
  • of larger plant fragments, and earthworm functions more as “soil
  • processors” that ingest and mix fi ne organic matter with soil as they
  • burrow. Specific food preferences and feeding mechanism differ
  • significantly.
  • Springtails and mites are vital components of soil ecosystem with a wide
  • range of diets, but mites show greater diversity, including specialized
  • parasitic and predatory roles. Both share detritivorous and some
  • herbivorous tendencies. Mites roles as significant pests and disease vectors
  • for both plants and animals.

questions.question: How does lignin content affect the decomposition of plant materials? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How does lignin content affect the decomposition of plant materials? [U]/ [CO2]
  • Higher lignin content slows down the decomposition of plant materials.
  • Lignin is a complex recalcitrant polymer that is difficult for microorganism
  • to breakdown: slows the rate, restricts access, requires speci alized enzymes
  • acts as a physical barrier, and contributes to recalcitrant pools.

questions.question: Describe characteristics of any five soil types. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe characteristics of any five soil types. [U]/ [CO5]
  • Sandy soil- weathered rock particles, large and loose, water drain quickly,
  • holds very little moisture or nutrients.
  • Clay soil- very fine particles, dense and poor at draining water, sticky when
  • wet and hard when dry
  • Silt soil- particles size are between clay and sand, smooth powdery texture,
  • holds more moisture than sand.
  • Loam soil – best for gardening balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay
  • along with organic matter; holds mo isture well , while also allowing for
  • good drainage.
  • Peat soil - dark and spongy formed from waterlogged around that has
  • accumulated a high amount of organic matter.

questions.question: How does soil type affect decomposition? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How does soil types affected decomposition? [U]/ [CO2]
  • By influencing factors like moisture, aeration, and pH, which impact
  • microbial activity. Sandy soils decompose slowly due to poor water and
  • nutrient retention. Clay soils can protect organic matter from
  • decomposition by forming aggregates that shield carbon stores from
  • microbes. Comp ost manure – rich soils decompose organic matter very
  • quickly because of their high moisture and nutrient content.

questions.question: Define field capacity in soils. / [CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Define field capacity in soils. [K]/ [CO5]
  • It is the amount of water held in soil after excess water has drained away by
  • gravity, typically 2 -3 days after rainfall or irrigations. It represents the
  • upper limit of plants available water where the soil is saturated but hot
  • waterlogged. Factors like soil texture, structure, organic matter and
  • temperature influence this value.
  • Field ca pacity is important for plant growth, irrigation management,
  • and nutrient availability.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the process of primary production in soils with reference to energy capture. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4, CO5]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the process of primary production in soils with reference to [U] / [CO1, CO2,
  • energy capture. CO3, CO4, CO5]
  • Primary production in soils is primarily a function of plant photosynthesis,
  • which captures solar energy and stores it as biomass, with a small
  • contribution from chemoantotrophic bacteria using chemical energy. The
  • captured energy enters the soil ecosystem mainly through plant roots and
  • the decomposition of organic matter. The dominant energy capture
  • mechanism is photosynthesis. The minor mechanism is chemosynthesis.
  • Primary production in soil is primarily an extension of above ground
  • plant activity, relying on solar energy capture and its subsequent transfer
  • below ground. The soil ecosystem acts as a critical hub for process ing,
  • cycling, and transferring this energy to support a vast and diverse
  • community of organisms.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Compare colonial growth forms and mycelial growth forms in terms of structure and function / [CO3] [4x8 = 32]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare colonial growth forms and mycelia growth forms in terms [U]/ [CO3]
  • of structure and function.
  • Soil microorganisms primarily exhibit growth in one of two forms mycelia
  • (filamentous) or colonial (unicellular/aggregates). These different
  • structures dictate their unique roles in the soil ecosystem, particularly in
  • nutrient cycling and soil structure formation.
  • Mycelial Growth Forms (Fungi and Actinomy cetes) : Structure -
  • filamentous network, large surface area, physical strength and long distance
  • transport Function – decomposition of complex organic matter, nutrient
  • cycling, symbiotic relationships (mycorrhizae), and disease suppression.
  • Colonial Growt h Forms (Most Bacteria and Algae) : Structure -
  • unicellular or simple aggregates, high abundance, motility and bio film
  • formation.
  • Function- fast nutrient cycling, nitrogen fixation and nitrification,
  • mineral solubilization, response to disturbance, and pat hogen
  • consumptions.
  • The mycelia form provides structural stability and is crucial for
  • breaking down tough organic materials and nutrient transport over large
  • distances, while the colonial form excels in rapid nutrient cycling and
  • diverse biochemical transformations in the soil microenvironment.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
